Abstract:
Today, we’re launching Particle to make highly optimized intelligence accessible to everyone. The cost of using capable models still limits who can use them, how often, and what they can build. We’re working to lower that cost by training models to solve problems more efficiently, so people can deploy more intelligence to solve more problems.

Particle-1, post-trained on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, sees large improvements in token efficiency using around ~45% fewer tokens on average across a wide variety of tasks. Many improvements in token optimization only improve on reducing costs but, in this case, tasks finish sooner which is good for end-users. We trained the model in reinforcement learning environments developed internally, with the goal of solving tasks with fewer tokens while maintaining accuracy.

This first release focuses on software engineering. We plan to bring Particle to other domains in future releases.

Training compute notes:
From tech report: "Mistral Large 4 was pretrained on 3,840 NVIDIA GB200 GPUs in a Mistral data center near Paris.
Our internal training stack is built on PyTorch and CUDA. Pretraining took 45 days, or about 4.15 million GPU-hours, with a model FLOPs utilization (MFU) of 36% and a goodput of 94.1%. Webmeasure MFU against peak hardware BF16 FLOP/s, include matrix-multiplication and attention
FLOPs."

GB200 is 2500 TFLOP/s BF16 peak, so 36% MFU and 94.1% goodput is 32.9% overall utilization. 
3840 * 45 * 24*3600 * 0.329 * 2500 trillion = 1.23e25 FLOP pretraining.

This suggests roughly 40T training tokens, using 6ND: 1.23e25 = 6* 52 billion * D.

For post-training, RL involved 162.5 billion output tokens during rollouts for RL, so RL FLOP was <1% of pre-training. SFT and mid-training tokens were not disclosed.

MFU is reported against bf16 spec, but report mentions FP8 in the pretraining without clarifying the primary format.
